proof_nl:
We prove a stronger statement by induction on r. For each positive integer r, let P(r) be: for every positive integer n there exists a vector w_{n,r}=(w_1,...,w_n) of positive integers with w_1>w_2>...>w_n such that for every real vector x=(x_1,...,x_n), Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)) = sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i and Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)) = sum_{i=1}^n w_{n+1-i} x_i. The lemma is exactly P(r) with n=m.

Base case r=1. Here Alt_1^+=(+1) and Alt_1^-=(-1), so T_{Alt_1^+}(x)=U(x) and T_{Alt_1^-}(x)=D(x). If x has length n, then by the definitions of U and D, Total(U(x)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} sum_{i=1}^{j-1} x_i = sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)x_i, because x_i appears in U(x)_j exactly when j>i, namely for n+1-i values of j. Likewise, Total(D(x)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} sum_{i=j}^{n} x_i = sum_{i=1}^n i x_i, because x_i appears in D(x)_j exactly when j<=i, namely for i values of j. Therefore P(1) holds with w_{n,1}=(n,n-1,...,1), which is a strictly decreasing vector of positive integers.

Inductive step. Assume P(r) holds for some r>=1. Fix a positive integer n. Apply P(r) with length n+1, and denote the resulting vector by v=(v_1,...,v_{n+1})=w_{n+1,r}. Then v_1>v_2>...>v_{n+1}>0, and for every real vector z of length n+1, Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(z)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_j z_j and Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(z)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_{n+2-j} z_j.

Define a length n vector w=(w_1,...,w_n) by w_i = sum_{k=1}^{n+1-i} v_k for 1<=i<=n. Since each v_k is a positive integer, each w_i is a positive integer. Also, for 1<=i<n, w_i-w_{i+1} = v_{n+1-i}>0, so w_1>w_2>...>w_n.

Now let x be any real vector of length n. Deleting the first sign from Alt_{r+1}^+ leaves Alt_r^-, so by the recursive definition of T_t, T_{Alt_{r+1}^+}(x)=T_{Alt_r^-}(U(x)). Hence Total(T_{Alt_{r+1}^+}(x)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_{n+2-j} U(x)_j = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_{n+2-j} sum_{i=1}^{j-1} x_i = sum_{i=1}^n (sum_{j=i+1}^{n+1} v_{n+2-j}) x_i = sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i, because sum_{j=i+1}^{n+1} v_{n+2-j} = sum_{k=1}^{n+1-i} v_k = w_i.

Similarly, deleting the first sign from Alt_{r+1}^- leaves Alt_r^+, so T_{Alt_{r+1}^-}(x)=T_{Alt_r^+}(D(x)). Therefore Total(T_{Alt_{r+1}^-}(x)) = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_j D(x)_j = sum_{j=1}^{n+1} v_j sum_{i=j}^{n} x_i = sum_{i=1}^{n} (sum_{j=1}^{i} v_j) x_i. But by the definition of w, w_{n+1-i} = sum_{k=1}^{i} v_k. Thus Total(T_{Alt_{r+1}^-}(x)) = sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{n+1-i} x_i.

So P(r+1) holds. By induction, P(r) is true for every positive integer r. Taking n=m gives the required vector w_{m,r}, and the lemma follows.
solver_summary: Proved by induction on the number r of alternating steps, in the stronger form valid for every input length n simultaneously. For r=1 the totals of U(x) and D(x) are explicit: coefficients are n,n-1,...,1 and their reverse. For the inductive step, use the coefficient vector v for length n+1 and r steps, then define the new length n vector by w_i = sum_{k=1}^{n+1-i} v_k. These are positive integers and strictly decreasing because w_i-w_{i+1}=v_{n+1-i}>0. Substituting z=U(x) for the plus-start case and z=D(x) for the minus-start case yields exactly the two required formulas.
vetter_reason: The induction is correct and complete. The base case r=1 computes Total(U(x)) and Total(D(x)) explicitly, yielding the claimed decreasing positive weights. In the inductive step, the proof correctly uses that removing the first sign from Alt_{r+1}^+ gives Alt_r^- and from Alt_{r+1}^- gives Alt_r^+, applies the induction hypothesis at length n+1, and defines new weights by partial sums of the previous ones. The coefficient calculations for both transformed totals are valid, and strict decrease follows from positivity of the previous weights. The proof matches the lemma statement exactly and is self-contained.
